summary: Lists the top-level domains that currently have address records (dotless domains) and provides a script to find them, as input for researchers considering the issues. It does not address policy.

plainLanguage.summary: A list of web names that have no dots, so people can study them.

subtitle: A catalog of DNS top-level domains with address records

tldr.problem: Researchers need to understand the extent of dotless domains (TLDs with A, AAAA, or MX records), as several organizations have raised concerns about their stability and security implications.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC lists all known dotless TLDs as of September 2013 and provides a shell script to identify them by querying the root zone.
tldr.outcome: The research community gained a baseline inventory of dotless domains to inform discussions about DNS stability and security policy.

today: RFC 7085 is an informational snapshot from 2013. While the specific list of dotless domains may have changed, the methodology in the RFC remains relevant for researchers studying DNS structure and TLD characteristics.

sections.title: The Dotless Domain Issue
sections.content:
The Internet Architecture Board and ICANN's Security and Stability Advisory Committee raised concerns about dotless domains, which are top-level domains that have address records (A, AAAA, or MX records) at the apex of the DNS tree. In normal DNS design, TLDs do not have such records.

However, many believed ICANN prohibited all dotless domains, which is not true; ICANN's policies apply only to their contracted TLDs. Country-code TLDs and other TLDs operate independently.

To help researchers understand the issue, this RFC provides a complete inventory of known dotless TLDs as of publication date and a reproducible script to find them in the future.
sections.plainLanguage: Most web domains are just directories that point to other places. Some are set up differently: they point directly to a computer. This document shows which ones do that.

sections.title: Scope and Methodology
sections.content:
This RFC defines a dotless domain as any TLD with an A, AAAA, or MX record at the apex. The RFC notes that several organizations (IAB, SSAC, NGPC) issued statements about dotless domains before this comprehensive inventory existed, but their concerns were not based on knowing the actual extent of the problem.

The authors conducted the first systematic survey to answer: exactly how many dotless domains exist, and which TLDs are they?
sections.plainLanguage: A dotless domain is a top-level domain that also acts like a computer address. The RFC surveys all of them.

sections.title: What the Survey Found
sections.content:
The survey checked every TLD in the root zone on September 3, 2013. About 5% of all TLDs have address records, and all of them are two-letter country-code TLDs (ccTLDs).

16 TLDs have A records (IPv4 addresses), including AC, AI, CM, DK, GG, IO, JE, KH, PN, SH, TK, TM, TO, UZ, VI, and WS. Only DK has an AAAA record (IPv6 address). A larger set of TLDs have MX records: AI, AX, CF, DM, GP, GT, HR, IO, KH, KM, LK, MQ, PA, TT, UA, VA, WS, and YE.

The RFC notes that the data remained stable for many months with few changes.
sections.plainLanguage: Out of hundreds of top-level domains, only about 17 have address records. They are all country domains like .io, .ws, or .tk.

sections.title: Finding Dotless Domains
sections.content:
The RFC includes a Bourne shell script that researchers can use to find dotless domains in the future. The script queries IANA's TLD list, resolves nameservers for each TLD, and then queries each nameserver for A, AAAA, and MX records.

The script checks each nameserver instead of doing simple queries because some TLD nameservers have inconsistent data. This methodical approach ensures reliable results. The RFC notes that the same methodology can be reused whenever researchers need updated dotless domain data.
sections.plainLanguage: The document includes a recipe for finding dotless domains yourself by asking DNS servers the right questions.
